pending_items.title: More than a third of Muslim students experience Islamophobia at UK universities, report finds
pending_items.content:
More than one in three Muslim students in the UK have experienced Islamophobia at university, with many facing abuse, threats and religious discrimination, according to a new report by the Federation of Student Islamic Societies (Fosis).

The report, titled "Belonging in Question" , found that 38 percent of Muslim students surveyed had experienced Islamophobia on campus, while 68 percent of those affected said they did not feel able to report what had happened to them.

Rahma Hegy, Fosis vice-president for student affairs, said Muslim students continued to make significant contributions to university life and wider British society, despite feeling unwelcome on campus.

"Many [students] tell us they do not feel they belong on the very campuses meant to include them," Hegy told Middle East Eye.

"They face discrimination, and too often they stay quiet because they do not expect anyone to be held accountable."

Hegy said the lack of accountability was among the organisation's greatest concerns and urged universities, student unions and the government to act on it.

The findings are based on responses from 715 students across 63 higher education institutions in the UK, making it one of the largest recent surveys of Muslim students' experiences at British universities.

Students described a range of incidents, including being spat at, receiving death threats and having urine thrown at them while wearing the hijab.

Others reported being excluded from laboratory sessions after requesting time to attend Friday prayers, being told to remove their hijab before undertaking clinical placements, and being called terrorists while attending peaceful vigils.

'They face discrimination, and too often they stay quiet because they do not expect anyone to be held accountable'

- Rahma Hegy, Federation of Islamic Student Societies

The report found that Muslim women were more likely to experience Islamophobia than men, with 42 percent reporting discrimination compared with 34 percent of male respondents.

Students at Russell Group universities, which include some of the UK's most prestigious institutions, also reported higher levels of Islamophobia.

Forty-four percent of those interviewed said they had experienced discrimination, compared with 34 percent at other universities.

The findings also highlighted concerns about the impact of the political climate surrounding Palestine on Muslim students' ability to express themselves.

Three in five respondents said they felt afraid or intimidated to express their views on Palestine.

The report further found that 45 percent of students who had experienced Islamophobia said it had a moderate to severe impact on their mental health.

Fosis said the findings demonstrated a need for universities, students' unions and the government to take more decisive action to address anti-Muslim discrimination and protect students' rights.

The organisation is calling on universities to formally recognise Islamophobia, adopt a definition and introduce mandatory awareness training for university staff and student leaders.

It also wants universities to introduce a dedicated Islamophobia category in their reporting systems, improve the accessibility of prayer arrangements and ensure that academic timetables and clinical placements accommodate Muslim students' religious obligations.

The report urges institutions to hold staff and students accountable for Islamophobic behaviour, while calling on the government and higher education sector to protect freedom of expression and reduce what it describes as the securitisation of university campuses.

Among its recommendations is a review of the government's Prevent duty, which requires public institutions, including universities, to have due regard to preventing people from being drawn into terrorism.

Former first minister of Scotland, Humza Yousaf, who wrote the foreword for the report, described the students' testimonies as being "as harrowing as they are infuriating".

"My family and I have been targeted with the most vile rape and death threats over the years, simply down to the faith we practice," said Yousaf.

"What we are witnessing, and what this report talks to, did not happen in a vacuum. I have warned time and again that too many in the political establishment were mainstreaming far-right hatred."

Yousaf called on universities to read the Fosis report as evidence rather than a complaint, arguing that the most "damning" finding is what happens after hostility occurs - where reporting barriers and weak institutional follow-through leave students without real change.

The Office for Students, which regulates higher education in England and monitors universities' compliance with the Prevent duty, had not responded to requests for comment at the time of publication.

Founded in 1963, Fosis is the national representative body for Muslim students in the UK and Ireland, bringing together more than 120 Islamic societies.

The report comes amid wider concerns about the treatment of pro-Palestinian activism in British universities, particularly following the outbreak of Israel's war on Gaza in October 2023.

Its findings raise questions about whether Muslim students can exercise their religious rights and freedom of political expression without facing discrimination or intimidation.

pending_items.title: Tortured into confessing: Report exposes abusive Israeli interrogation of Palestinians
pending_items.content:
In 2021, Israeli police arrested a Palestinian man known as R, who after multiple rounds of torture, signed a confession document for a crime he did not commit.

He is one of hundreds of Palestinians featured in a report by the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel (PCATI) who faced criminal proceedings on the basis of confessions extracted under duress.

The man, whose name was withheld for fear of reprisals, spent months in prison before video footage showed he had been nowhere near the scene of the crime he was accused of.

Before that video came to light, R repeatedly tried to withdraw his confession to the unspecified crime but was tortured by Shin Bet officials regardless.

He and his brother, who had also faced charges, eventually secured acquittals and their release.

Theirs was a rare case of acquittal within an Israeli justice system where torture, sexual assault, rape and inhuman treatment have become normalised, according to multiple reports from human rights organisations and the UN.

In its report, PCATI profiled 42 cases it had filed over the past decade on behalf of Palestinians who reported torture during Shin Bet interrogations.

In 33 of those cases, Palestinian detainees confessed under torture during or after questioning.

Israeli courts only recognised four of those confessions as false, despite interrogators using torture on the detainees.

The report describes how a confession extracted under duress can make its way into a criminal case.

Israel does not examine the circumstances preceding a detainee’s confession when deciding whether they gave it “freely and voluntarily”, unlike other developed countries that explicitly ban torture and the use of any evidence obtained using it.

In one case, a journalist identified as M said she signed a police confession to stop the torture of her brother, whom interrogators had threatened.

She later pleaded guilty to a charge involving prohibited political activity.

In one case, official records showed that Shin Bet interrogated a Palestinian lawyer for about 552 hours over 27 and a half days, an average of 20 hours a day.

The lawyer, identified as TB, told an Israeli judge their client was in severe pain and could barely sleep. The court extended his detention.

The justice ministry unit that reviewed his complaint said interrogators had obtained the required authorisations to interrogate the man and declined to open a criminal investigation into the torture.

More than 1,680 complaints of abuse during interrogation reached the Israeli justice ministry’s oversight unit between 2001 and 2024, according to official figures obtained through freedom of information requests and cited in the report.

The unit recommended criminal investigations in five cases. Authorities closed all five files without an indictment.

In May of this year, the United Nations added Israel to its blacklist for sexual violence in conflict zones.

The move follows multiple reports by human rights organisations and media outlets - including Middle East Eye - documenting allegations of rape and other forms of sexual violence by Israeli forces against Palestinians since October 2023.

Israeli soldiers and prison guards have faced allegations of a wide range of abuses against Palestinian detainees since October 2023, including rape, torture, starvation and degrading treatment.

At least 100 prisoners have reportedly died in custody under these conditions, with nearly half dying in military detention and the remainder in facilities run by the IPS.

Dozens of testimonies from released detainees have detailed alleged mistreatment in Israeli custody.

In December, two Palestinians held in separate Israeli prisons told MEE they had suffered violent sexual assault.

One detainee said his jailers dragged him into a room where, for nearly an hour, they kicked, stamped on, insulted and raped him with an object while he wore a blindfold.

The other said trained military dogs raped him.

Last year, a UN inquiry accused Israel of using sexualised torture and rape as "a method of war... to destabilize, dominate, oppress and destroy the Palestinian people".

The Israeli human rights organisation B’Tselem has described the Israeli prison system as a "network of torture camps" within which guards and soldiers subjected prisoners to the "repeated use of sexual violence", including "gang sexual violence and assault committed by a group of prison guards or soldiers".
